name: Purchase Ladder
tagline: An ordered sequence of separately bought offers where a later position stays locked until every purchase beneath it has been made.
desc: A purchase ladder orders two or more separately acquired offers so that a position higher up cannot be taken until every position beneath it has been acquired, and at least one of those lower positions requires an actual purchase. Reaching a stated endpoint therefore costs the sum of whatever was bought below it, regardless of what price sits on the endpoint itself, even a free one. What makes this a distinct mechanic rather than ordinary pricing is the lock: a shelf of currency packages or subscription tiers that can each be bought directly, in any order, however steeply priced or however clearly the largest is marked best value, is not a purchase ladder. The same shelf becomes one the moment a tier can only be reached by first buying the tier below it.
principle: The purchase is the advancement. Nothing the product does on its own moves the user up the sequence; only buying the position beneath the next one does.
warn: The label is easy to misapply toward an ordinary tiered price list: ascending prices, a best-value badge, and a shelf deliberately arranged to steer the buyer upward are all ordinary price design, and none of them is this mechanic without an actual lock stopping a later tier from being bought on its own. The risk runs the other way too: a free or cheap-looking position at the top of a locked sequence is easy to read as a giveaway, when its real price is the sum of everything purchased to reach it.
variants: Fully paid ladder, every position in the sequence requires a purchase, and each one unlocks the next
Mixed ladder, free and purchased positions sit on either side of one another, with at least one purchase still standing between the user and the positions above it
Free-endpoint ladder, the terminal position is free or nominally priced and is reached only by purchasing the positions below it
Threshold ladder, a position opens after a stated number of purchases of a repeatable offer rather than after one named position
Variable-content ladder, the contents of one or more positions aren't fully resolved before that position is acquired
lifecycle: Needs at least two separately acquired offers and a purchase already standing as a condition on one of them before there's a sequence to speak of. Most consequential once a user is looking at a visible endpoint they can't yet reach, with the cost of getting there already spent below it rather than stated on the position itself.
